newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl offers more tax talks to divided SPD.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl offers more tax talks to divided SPD.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday seized on rifts opening among Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to try and resuscitate cross-party talks on tax reforms which had looked as good as dead less than a week ago.
Kohl told regional leaders of his Christian Democrat party (CDU) he was ready to talk to SPD leaders "day or night", and even to meet opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine face to face.
"I am always ready to meet Herr Lafontaine. I'm not afraid of contact," Kohl said in the Baltic port of Warnemuende.

Since the collapse last week of talks on government plans to axe 30 billion marks ($17 billion) in tax, some politicians have been sounding out ways to break the logjam that has become the latest point of discord in deadlocked Bonn.

Germany's bid to reform its tax system has no direct link with Bonn's effort to qualify this year for European monetary union, but the government wants to encourage investment and job create to help shore up state finances over the longer term.

Recent comments by some SPD state leaders indicate they do not stand four-square behind Lafontaine's hard line on tax, and may make concessions when coalition tax bills reach the SPD-led upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, this summer.
The Bundesrat has the power to block most tax legislation.

Hamburg Mayor Henning Voscherau said the SPD must agree to slash the top income tax rate from 53 percent, a Kohl plan Lafontaine has denounced in what sound like premature campaign speeches for next year's general election.
"We have no choice but to come to an agreement on the peak rate," he told ARD television on Tuesday morning.

This pragmatic approach echoed comments by Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder -- Lafontaine's main rival for the privilege of running against Kohl in the October poll -- and a couple of other SPD state premiers.
"Sometimes it is overlooked that there are great problems with the tax reform, but we have to try to reach a compromise," Schroeder said on Monday.
Despite their conciliatory tone on tax, the SPD barons have dismissed talk of a split opening up in their party.

Schroeder said the government could not try to "divide and conquer" the SPD. Voscherau later dismissed as "Bonn rumours" reports of a wedge being driven between Lafontaine and his advisors. "This is a red herring," he said in a statement.

Politicians earned a stinging rebuke from President Roman Herzog at the weekend for indulging in a political blockade which he said was thwarting reforms to boost growth and cut unemployment now standing at 4.5 million.

Commentators have said Lafontaine's tough tax stand was to blame for the failure of the talks. But Lafontaine has showed no sign of backing down, saying government legislation had "no chance because it cannot be financed".
Lafontaine has already moved to get the party to back his refusal to cut the top rate of income tax. In a letter to SPD functionaries he said the party could not agree to "tax giveaways to the rich".

The emerging differences between Lafontaine -- who is also premier in the tiny Saarland state on the French border -- could end up playing a decisive part in deciding who ends up leading the party into the 1998 vote.
Schroeder -- a pragmatic moderate compared by commentators to Britain's Tony Blair -- could get a big boost if Labour wins by a healthy margin at this Thursday's election.
The pro-business Schroeder has also been riding high in opinion polls, which show he would beat Kohl in a head-to-head direct vote. Lafontaine would lose.

Sixty-eight percent of those surveyed by the Emnid research group for this week's Spiegel news weekly said they would like to see Schroeder playing an important role in Germany's future, a rise of nine points on the previous poll.

Kohl was stable on 45 percent, while Lafontaine's rating fell eight points to 44 percent after the collapse of the tax talks. "Confidence in parties and politicians has fallen...only Schroeder could collect plus points," Spiegel wrote.
($ = 1.730 German Marks)
